title: Lesson 55: Scaling Agent Workloads: Horizontal Scaling, Queues, and Worker Pools
description: Adding capacity to an agent system by running more workers, decoupling producers from consumers with a queue, and sizing the worker pool off queue measurements within rate and budget limits.

questions.question: Why must an agent worker be stateless for horizontal scaling to help?
options: Because a worker can only call a model provider when it is stateless
Because context held in one worker's memory ties it there
Because stateless workers use no memory while they run
Because state is never allowed in any distributed system
questions.explanation: If each request's context is held in a worker's memory, that worker is the only one that can finish it, so extra copies cannot help. The state has to live somewhere any worker can reach.

questions.question: Which queue measurement is the honest signal for when to add workers?
options: A steady empty queue with idle workers
A high completion rate with low CPU use on the workers
A growing backlog whose wait time keeps climbing
A latency budget that is comfortably under target
questions.explanation: Scaling is driven by backlog: growing queue depth and rising wait time mean workers cannot pick work up fast enough. An empty queue with idle workers is the signal to scale down, not up.

questions.question: Which pair of hard caps keeps a scaling worker pool from spending without limit?
options: A maximum pool size and a task-level rate limit
A minimum replica count and a fixed batch size
A maximum thread count and an unlimited daily budget
A fixed memory request and a disabled quota
questions.explanation: A pool that scales up forever can overshoot the provider's quota or the budget, so you cap the number of workers and rate-limit executions against the model endpoint. Both are security and cost controls, not just billing hygiene.
